title: 2019 AMC 12A Problem 24
statement: For how many integers \(n\) between \(1\) and \(50,\) inclusive, is \[ \dfrac{(n^2 - 1)!}{(n!)^n} \] an integer? (Recall that \(0! = 1.\))

solutions.text:
Fix a prime \(p\le n.\) By Legendre’s formula, the difference between the exponent of \(p\) in the numerator and its exponent in the denominator is \[ \begin{aligned} D_p &=\sum_{k\ge1}\left\lfloor\dfrac{n^2-1}{p^k}\right\rfloor\\ &\quad-n\sum_{k\ge1}\left\lfloor\dfrac{n}{p^k}\right\rfloor. \end{aligned} \] If \(r_k\) is the remainder of \(n\) modulo \(p^k,\) the \(k\)th summand is \(\left\lfloor\dfrac{nr_k-1}{p^k}\right\rfloor.\)

Let \(a=v_p(n).\) The first \(a\) summands are \(-1.\) If \(n\) is not a power of \(p,\) write \(n=p^a m\) with \(m\ge2.\) When \(a\ge1,\) the next summand is at least \(\dfrac{n}{p}-1\ge a,\) and all later summands are nonnegative; when \(a=0,\) every summand is already nonnegative. Thus \(D_p\ge0\) unless \(n\) is a power of \(p.\)

For \(n=p^a,\) Legendre’s formula reduces the requirement to \(p^a-1\ge2a(p-1).\) Among prime powers at most \(50,\) this fails exactly when \(a=1\) (so \(n\) is prime) and when \(n=2^2=4.\) There are \(15\) primes at most \(50,\) plus \(n=4,\) giving \(16\) failures. Hence \(50 - 16 = 34\) values of \(n\) work.

Thus, the correct answer is D.
hints: Compare the exponent of a prime \(p\) in numerator and denominator using \(v_p(m!) = \dfrac{m - s_p(m)}{p - 1}\)
Failure requires \(n\) to be a prime power \(p^a\) with \(p^a - 1 \lt 2a(p - 1)\)
